WAGE GARNISHMENT (EARNINGS WITHHOLDING ORDER) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

EARNINGS WITHHOLDING ORDER PROCESSING DECLARATION
Employer: Acme Corp
Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Judgment creditor: Acme Collections LLC
Court case number: CGC-26-123456
Levying officer: San Francisco County Sheriff
Date earnings withholding order served on employer: October 1, 2026
Total amount stated in the order as required to satisfy the judgment: $5,000
Employee's disposable earnings used for this calculation: $1,200
Pay period type used for this calculation: weekly
Applicable state or local minimum hourly wage used for this calculation: $16.50

Calculation basis: The withholding amount above was calculated using the lesser-of formula and pay-period multiplier set out in Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050, applied to the disposable earnings and minimum-wage figures stated above — or, if the order served is a withholding order for support, the different formula set out in Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052. This declaration is a record of the order's terms and of the inputs used to calculate the withholding amount for Acme Corp's payroll file. It states facts about the order and the calculation; it is not a determination of Acme Corp's or Jordan Alex Lee's legal rights or obligations under the order.

THE WAGE GARNISHMENT LAW AND HOW AN EMPLOYER BECOMES OBLIGATED TO WITHHOLD
California's Wage Garnishment Law generally makes the earnings withholding order the exclusive judicial procedure for requiring an employer to withhold an employee's earnings to pay a debt — the one stated exception is an earning assignment order for support. Once a judgment creditor has an earnings withholding order issued and it is served on Acme Corp as Jordan Alex Lee's employer, Acme Corp is required by statute to comply with it; if Acme Corp is served with more than one earnings withholding order, the statute requires compliance with whichever order was served first (subject to separate priority rules for support and tax orders and certain elder-financial-abuse orders).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except for an earning assignment order for support, the earnings of an employee shall not be required to be withheld by an employer for payment of a debt by means of any judicial procedure other than pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.020 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.020 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.020.)
  "An employer shall comply with the first earnings withholding order served upon the employer."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.023(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.023, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.023.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutory framework (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 706.020, 706.023(a)), offered as documented evidence of what California's Wage Garnishment Law says — not a claim about which state's procedure governs a specific employer or employee; wage garnishment procedure varies significantly by state, and federal law separately governs garnishment for certain federal debts (e.g., student loans, taxes) outside this state framework entirely. The two citations are from different sections of the same chapter (§ 706.020 and § 706.023), not subsections of one section, so they are treated as independent sources. Separately, California's primary mechanism for collecting child or spousal support from wages is not this earnings-withholding-order framework but a distinct 'earnings assignment order' issued under the Family Code, which by statute takes priority over an ordinary earnings withholding order (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.031) — that separate framework was not independently verified for this clause set and is not the subject of this document. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

THE GENERAL WITHHOLDING LIMIT: THE LESSER-OF FORMULA
For a general (non-support) earnings withholding order, California law caps the amount that may be withheld from Jordan Alex Lee's disposable earnings for any workweek at the lesser of two figures: 20% of Jordan Alex Lee's disposable earnings for that week, or 40% of the amount by which Jordan Alex Lee's disposable earnings for that week exceed 48 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect when the earnings are payable (or 48 times the local minimum hourly wage, if the applicable local minimum wage is higher than the state minimum wage). Separate multipliers apply to convert this weekly formula to daily, biweekly, semimonthly, and monthly pay periods.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the maximum amount of disposable earnings of an individual judgment debtor for any workweek that is subject to levy under an earnings withholding order shall not exceed the lesser of the following: (1) Twenty percent of the individual’s disposable earnings for that week. (2) Forty percent of the amount by which the individual’s disposable earnings for that week exceed 48 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect at the time the earnings are payable."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.050.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision currently says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The federal default limit under the Consumer Credit Protection Act is materially different and less protective of the debtor: 25% of disposable earnings, or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage, whichever is less (15 U.S.C. § 1673(a)) — California's 20%/48-times formula supersedes the federal default for debts collected in California courts because federal law expressly permits a state to impose a lower maximum. The current California formula (20% / 48-times-minimum-wage) took effect operatively on September 1, 2023, under a 2022 amendment (Stats. 2022, Ch. 849 (SB 1477)), which repealed and replaced a prior version of this section that had tied the exempt amount to federal poverty guidelines rather than to a multiple of the minimum wage; a document or calculation relying on the pre-September-2023 formula is relying on superseded law. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 706.050(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text. This clause states the general, non-support limit only; a materially different and generally higher cap applies where the order is a withholding order for support, addressed in a separate clause. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

THE DIFFERENT, HIGHER CAP FOR A WITHHOLDING ORDER FOR SUPPORT
Where the earnings withholding order served on Acme Corp is a withholding order for support (a distinct sub-type of earnings withholding order used to collect delinquent child or spousal support), the general 20%-or-40%-over-the-minimum-wage limit does not apply. Instead, California law exempts one-half of Jordan Alex Lee's disposable earnings from levy under this framework, and any interested party may move the court for an equitable division of Jordan Alex Lee's earnings that accounts for the needs of everyone Jordan Alex Lee is required to support — but a court-ordered division under that equitable-division authority cannot exceed the cap set by federal law, which permits withholding up to 50% of disposable earnings (or 55% if the arrears being collected are more than twelve weeks old) where Jordan Alex Lee is supporting a current spouse or dependent child, and up to 60% (or 65% for arrears more than twelve weeks old) where Jordan Alex Lee is not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "one-half of the disposable earnings (as defined by Section 1672 of Title 15 of the United States Code) of the judgment debtor, plus any amount withheld from the judgment debtor’s earnings pursuant to any earnings assignment order for support, is exempt from levy under this chapter where the earnings withholding order is a withholding order for support under Section 706.030."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.052.)
  "The maximum part of the aggregate disposable earnings of an individual for any workweek which is subject to garnishment to enforce any order for the support of any person shall not exceed— (A) where such individual is supporting his spouse or dependent child (other than a spouse or child with respect to whose support such order is used), 50 per centum of such individual’s disposable earnings for that week; and (B) where such individual is not supporting such a spouse or dependent child described in clause (A), 60 per centum of such individual’s disposable earnings for that week"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1673(b)(2) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 15 U.S.C. § 1673(b)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1673)
  Known gap: This clause combines one state statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052(a)) and one federal statute (15 U.S.C. § 1673(b)(2)) — different sovereigns and different code sections, so they are independent sources, not duplicates of a single source. This is one state's mechanism for the specific 'withholding order for support' sub-type defined within the Wage Garnishment Law (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.030) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support obligation, and not a description of California's more commonly used child/spousal support collection tool. That more commonly used tool is the Family Code 'earnings assignment order for support,' which is a separate mechanism that, by statute, takes priority over any earnings withholding order (including a withholding order for support) when both reach an employer (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.031) — the Family Code provisions governing that separate mechanism were not independently verified for this clause set. The federal statute quoted here is a nationwide ceiling on support garnishment generally, applicable regardless of which state-law collection mechanism is used; it does not by itself specify which mechanism a given support order proceeds through. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

WHEN WITHHOLDING MUST BEGIN AND WHEN WITHHELD AMOUNTS MUST BE REMITTED
Under California law, the withholding period generally begins on the 30th day after an earnings withholding order is served on Acme Corp; if a claim of exemption is filed with the levying officer and Acme Corp receives actual notice of it before the close of business on the 29th day after service, the withholding period instead begins on the 45th day after service. Once the withholding period has begun, Acme Corp must withhold the required amount from all of Jordan Alex Lee's earnings payable for any pay period ending within that period. California law separately requires Acme Corp to pay the amounts withheld to the levying officer monthly, no later than the 15th day of each month, unless Acme Corp elects to pay more frequently, in which case payment for a given pay period is due within 10 days after that pay period closes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "As used in this section, “withholding period” means the period which commences on the 30th day after service of an earnings withholding order upon the judgment debtor’s employer. If a claim of exemption is filed with the levying officer, and the employer is given actual notice before the close of business on the 29th day after the service of the earnings withholding order on the judgment debtor’s employer, the withholding period commences on the 45th day after service of the earnings withholding order on the judgment debtor’s employer."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.022(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.022, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.022.)
  "the amount required to be withheld pursuant to an earnings withholding order shall be paid monthly to the levying officer not later than the 15th day of each month"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.025(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.025, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.025.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 706.022(a), 706.025), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's payroll timing; other states set different deadlines for withholding to begin and for remitting withheld amounts. The two citations are from different sections of the same chapter (§ 706.022 and § 706.025), not subsections of one section, so they are treated as independent sources. This clause states the general timing rule; it does not address the separate rules governing when a withholding period may be dormant, suspended, or terminated, or the priority rules that apply when more than one order or assignment reaches the same employer. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION: DISCHARGE BASED ON GARNISHMENT
California law prohibits Acme Corp from discharging Jordan Alex Lee because Jordan Alex Lee's wages have been threatened with garnishment, and separately prohibits Acme Corp from discharging Jordan Alex Lee because Jordan Alex Lee's wages have been garnished for the payment of one judgment; an employment contract term giving Jordan Alex Lee less protection than this statute provides is void as against public policy. Federal law contains a related but differently worded protection: it prohibits an employer from discharging an employee because the employee's earnings have been garnished for any one indebtedness, and makes a willful violation punishable by a fine, imprisonment, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No employer may discharge any employee by reason of the fact that his wages have been subjected to garnishment for the payment of one judgment. A provision of a contract of employment that provides an employee with less protection than is provided by this subdivision is against public policy and void."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 2929, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2929.)
  "No employer may discharge any employee by reason of the fact that his earnings have been subjected to garnishment for any one indebtedness."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1674(a) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 15 U.S.C. § 1674(a) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1674)
  Known gap: This clause combines one state statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(b)) and one federal statute (15 U.S.C. § 1674(a)) — different sovereigns, so they are independent sources. California's statute expressly states it is intended to aid enforcement of, and to be interpreted consistently with, the federal Consumer Credit Protection Act's anti-discharge provisions (Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(e)), but the two statutes are not identically worded: California's protects against discharge for garnishment 'for the payment of one judgment,' while the federal provision protects against discharge for garnishment 'for any one indebtedness.' Neither statute's quoted text expressly extends this specific protection to discharge based on multiple garnishments for different debts arriving at or near the same time — that scenario is simply not addressed by the text quoted here, and this clause does not assert that either statute resolves it. This is a general statement of what these two statutes say; it is not a case-by-case assessment of whether a particular discharge was lawful. No case law was researched for this clause given CourtListener's daily rate limit and the statutory clarity of the text itself; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

EMPLOYER LIABILITY TO THE JUDGMENT CREDITOR FOR NONCOMPLIANCE
If Acme Corp fails to withhold, or fails to pay over to the levying officer, an amount Acme Corp is required to withhold and pay over under a validly served earnings withholding order, California law allows the judgment creditor to bring a civil action against Acme Corp to recover that amount, and this remedy is not the judgment creditor's exclusive one. The same statute also protects an employer on the other side of this rule: an employer that complies with a written order or written notice that purports to have been given or served under this chapter is not subject to civil or criminal liability for that compliance, unless the employer actively participated in a fraud.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employer fails to withhold or to pay over the amount the employer is required to withhold and pay over pursuant to this chapter, the judgment creditor may bring a civil action against the employer to recover such amount. The remedy provided by this subdivision is not exclusive."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.154.)
  "an employer who complies with any written order or written notice which purports to be given or served in accordance with the provisions of this chapter is not subject to any civil or criminal liability for such compliance unless the employer has actively participated in a fraud."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=706.154.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154). Both citations in this clause come from subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent, sources for verification purposes. The statutory text authorizes the judgment creditor to recover 'such amount' — meaning the amount the employer failed to withhold and pay over — from the employer; it does not itself state a separate fixed statutory penalty on top of that amount, so a document or calculation assuming a specific additional penalty figure beyond the shortfall amount is going beyond what this text says. This clause is not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's liability, and it does not address any separate liability an employer might have under other law (for example, wage-and-hour statutes) for the same underlying failure. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
By signing below, the undersigned certifies, on behalf of Acme Corp, that the information stated in this earnings withholding order processing declaration is accurate to the best of the signer's knowledge as of the date signed below.

Signed: _______________________________________________
Jordan Alex Lee
On behalf of Acme Corp
Date: October 1, 2026

Both citations in this clause come from subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent, sources for verification purposes. The statutory text authorizes the judgment creditor to recover 'such amount' — meaning the amount the employer failed to withhold and pay over — from the employer; it does not itself state a separate fixed statutory penalty on top of that amount, so a document or calculation assuming a specific additional penalty figure beyond the shortfall amount is going beyond what this text says. This clause is not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's liability, and it does not address any separate liability an employer might have under other law (for example, wage-and-hour statutes) for the same underlying failure. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.
